fields.Back: Energy the source supplies per unit charge
fields.SpeakFront: definition of the emf, epsilon, of a source
fields.SpeakBack: the energy the source supplies per unit charge
fields.Elaboration: Measured in volts. It's not a force, despite the name "electromotive force".

fields.Front: Terminal voltage of a real emf source (emf \(\varepsilon\), internal resistance \(r\)) delivering current \(I\)
fields.SpeakFront: terminal voltage of a real emf source, with emf epsilon and internal resistance r, delivering current I
fields.Elaboration: Equals \(\varepsilon\) only when \(I=0\) or the source is ideal. Under a short circuit, \(r\) sets the current.

fields.Front: Equivalent resistance of resistors in series
fields.SpeakFront: equivalent resistance of resistors in series
fields.SpeakBack: the sum, R one plus R two and so on
fields.Elaboration: The same current flows through each, and the voltage drops add.

golden.note: 'Series' vs 'parallel' in the prompts is the interference guard.

fields.Front: Why do voltage drops add for resistors in series?
fields.Back: Energy conservation: a charge loses \(qV_1\), then \(qV_2\), then \(qV_3\) going from a to b, which totals \(q(V_a-V_b)\)
fields.SpeakFront: why do voltage drops add for resistors in series?
fields.SpeakBack: energy conservation; a charge loses q V one, then q V two, then q V three between the ends, which totals q times the whole potential difference
fields.Elaboration: With the same \(I\) through each, \(IR_{eq}=IR_1+IR_2+IR_3\) gives the series rule.

golden.note: Answers 'what does this mean?' with the conservation law the slide mentions but doesn't explain.

fields.Front: Equivalent resistance of resistors in parallel
fields.SpeakFront: equivalent resistance of resistors in parallel
fields.SpeakBack: one over R equivalent equals one over R one, plus one over R two, and so on
fields.Elaboration: The same voltage is across each, and the currents add (charge conservation). \(R_{eq}\) is less than the smallest resistor.

golden.note: The 'less than the smallest' check in Elaboration catches inverted answers.

fields.Back: Current into a junction equals current out: \(\sum I_\text{in}=\sum I_\text{out}\)
fields.SpeakBack: the current into a junction equals the current out

golden.note: Revision: the rule, split from its conservation law.

fields.Elaboration: In steady state, charge can't pile up at a junction.

fields.SpeakFront: Kirchhoff's junction rule follows from which conservation law?

golden.note: Revision: the reason half. The rule's name in the prompt keeps it apart from the loop-rule card (canon 14).

fields.Back: The potential changes around any closed loop sum to zero: \(\sum\Delta V=0\)
fields.Elaboration: Use it when series/parallel reduction doesn't work, e.g. two sources in different branches.
fields.SpeakBack: the potential changes around any closed loop add to zero

golden.note: Revision: the rule, split from its conservation law.

fields.Elaboration: \(V\) is potential energy per charge, and a charge that goes around a loop returns to the same potential.

fields.Situation: Writing a loop equation that crosses a resistor against the assumed current direction
fields.Fix: Against the current, the potential rises: \(+IR\). With the current it's \(-IR\). Crossing a battery from − to + gives \(+\varepsilon\).
fields.Why: Potential drops in the direction current flows through a resistor. A wrong initial guess of direction just shows up as a negative \(I\).
fields.SpeakSituation: writing a loop equation that crosses a resistor against the assumed current direction
fields.SpeakFix: against the current the potential rises, so plus I R; with the current it is minus I R; crossing a battery from minus to plus is plus epsilon

fields.Elaboration: From \(P=VI\) with \(V=IR\). Handy in series, where \(I\) is shared.

fields.Front: Resistance of a uniform conductor (length \(L\), cross-section \(A\), resistivity \(\rho\))
fields.SpeakFront: resistance of a uniform conductor with length L, cross section A, and resistivity rho
fields.Elaboration: Longer means more resistance; fatter means less. Resistivity is a material property, resistance is a property of the object.

fields.Front: Ohm's law in its general (microscopic) form
fields.SpeakFront: Ohm's law in its general, microscopic form
fields.SpeakBack: current density J equals sigma E, which is E over rho
fields.Elaboration: Integrate over a uniform wire to get \(V=IR\) with \(R=\rho L/A\).

golden.note: The Elaboration links the micro and macro forms instead of carding V = IR again.

fields.Front: Conventional current direction, relative to potential and to \(\vec E\)
fields.Back: The direction positive charge would flow: toward decreasing potential, along \(\vec E\)
fields.SpeakFront: conventional current direction, relative to potential and to the electric field
fields.SpeakBack: the direction positive charge would flow; toward decreasing potential, along the field
fields.Elaboration: Electrons actually drift the other way. Inside an emf source, current goes from low to high potential.
